what_it_does: Running an AI language model on a GPU becomes slow when the model generates tokens one by one, because each step must fetch enormous amounts of data from memory chips and the math units sit mostly idle. Pimba moves small computing engines physically inside the memory chips so that arithmetic happens where the data lives, cutting out the slow round-trip to the GPU. It also uses a compact number format called MX8 — numbers stored in groups sharing a single common scaling value — that preserves accuracy while shrinking the data enough to fit the memory-bandwidth budget.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Modern language models that use recurrent or state-space designs (alternatives to transformers such as Mamba-2, RetNet, and HGRN2) maintain a 'state matrix' — a fixed-size running summary of everything seen so far. Updating that matrix every token requires reading and writing it entirely from the memory chip, making it memory-bandwidth-bound. The same is true for the key-value store (a record of past token representations) in standard transformer models.

How it works. Pimba places small processors, called State-update Processing Units (SPUs), directly inside the memory chip rather than out on the GPU. Each SPU handles four operations in a pipeline: (1) fetch the current state from the memory row buffer (the temporary holding area inside the chip), (2) multiply the state by a decay factor and simultaneously compute the outer product (a way to combine two vectors into a matrix) of two input vectors, (3) add those two results together to form the new state, (4) perform a final matrix-times-vector multiplication to produce the output, then write the updated state back.

The key design choice. Each SPU is shared between two memory banks instead of one. While bank A is being read (feeding the SPU), bank B is writing its completed result — then they swap roles. This interleaving trick keeps the SPU busy every cycle without needing one unit per bank, halving the hardware area while matching the throughput of a per-bank design.

The number format. State values are stored in MX8 — groups of 16 numbers sharing one 8-bit scaling exponent, with small extra bits adjusting each pair within the group. Standard floating-point formats lose tiny values through a 'swamping' effect during repeated accumulation, breaking accuracy. MX8's structure avoids this, and the paper adds stochastic rounding (randomly rounding up or down with probabilities that preserve the average) to recover even more accuracy.

The result. Compared to a standard GPU, Pimba reduces state-update latency by 14.6×, translating to up to 4.1× more tokens generated per second. Compared to an existing in-memory processor (HBM-PIM), the speedup is 2.1×.
